newsitem.title: USA: Trial of reputed New York mob boss begins.
newsitem.headline: Trial of reputed New York mob boss begins.

text.p: The long-awaited trial of Vincent "The Chin" Gigante opened on Wednesday, with prosecutors calling the reputed mob boss a "cold-blooded killer" who has faked mental illness to avoid prosecution.

Gigante was wheeled in a wheelchair into a federal court in Brooklyn, a borough of New York City, where he sat quietly during the trial's opening arguments. Unshaven, he appeared to nod off frequently.
"This case is about a powerful Mafia boss and the great lengths he would go to to protect his position in one of the most successful Mafia gangs," said Assistant U.S. Attorney George Stamboulidis.
"It's about cold-blooded murders he ordered to be carried out," he said.
The reputed head of the Genovese crime family faces a 21-count murder and racketeering indictment.

The start of the trial comes seven years after Gigante, 69, was arrested. Since then, defence attorneys have argued he was mentally ill and unable to stand trial, but federal court Judge Jack Weinstein ruled the trial should proceed.
Stamboulidis characterised Gigante as a shrewd mob boss who began feigning mental illness in the 1960s.

Gigante is accused of ordering the murders of seven people and conspiring to kill three others. He ordered the murders to avenge breaches of organised crime protocol, including unauthorised slayings, the prosecutor said.
One Gigante target was John Gotti, the reputed head of the rival Gambino family, he said.
The order to kill Gotti was for the unsanctioned murder of Gambino boss Paul Castellano, he said. Gotti has been convicted of murder and is serving a life prison sentence.

Defence attorney Michael Marinaccio said the trial will allow jurors to "separate fact from fiction, the man from the myth." He portrayed Gigante as a "neighborhood guy" who spent most of his time walking the streets around his Greenwich Village home.
Gigante earned the nicknames "The Oddfather" and "The Robe" for his habit of wearing a bathrobe while wandering around and mumbling to himself.
In an agreement with the judge, Gigante must wear street clothes to his trial. The deal also allows doctors to monitor Gigante's condiditon, and once on Wednesday they gave him heart medication.
The first testimony came from an FBI agent who said he followed Gigante and watched him make calls from pay telephones.
